claim: Beta oscillations (15-29Hz) are among the most prominent signatures of brain activity.
source: Beta oscillations (15-29Hz) are among the most prominent signatures of brain activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about beta oscillations presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Beta power is predictive of healthy and abnormal behaviors, including perception, attention and motor action.
source: Beta power is predictive of healthy and abnormal behaviors, including perception, attention and motor action.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing multiple prior studies.

claim: In non-averaged signals, beta can emerge as transient high-power 'events'.
source: In non-averaged signals, beta can emerge as transient high-power 'events'.
evidence: This is demonstrated through data presented in Figure 2 showing individual trial spectrograms.

claim: Functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power in primary somatosensory neocortex reflect a difference in the number of high-power beta events per trial (event rate).
source: We show that functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power in primary somatosensory neocortex reflect a difference in the number of high-power beta events per trial, i.e. event rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Beta events occurring close to the stimulus were more likely to impair perception.
source: Further, beta events occurring close to the stimulus were more likely to impair perception.
evidence: This finding is supported by data in Figure 8 showing timing relationships between beta events and detection performance.

claim: The results on beta event rate predicting behavior are consistent across detection and attention tasks in human magnetoencephalography.
source: These results are consistent across detection and attention tasks in human magnetoencephalography
evidence: Data from both human detection and attention tasks are presented throughout the results section, particularly in Figures 1, 6, 7, and 8.

claim: The results on beta event rate predicting behavior are consistent in local field potentials from mice performing a detection task.
source: and in local field potentials from mice performing a detection task.
evidence: Mouse LFP data are presented throughout the results section in parallel with human data, particularly in Figures 1, 6, 7, and 8.

claim: An increased propensity of beta events predicts the failure to effectively transmit information through specific neocortical representations.
source: These results imply that an increased propensity of beta events predicts the failure to effectively transmit information through specific neocortical representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings showing negative correlation between beta event rate and detection/attention performance.

claim: Modulations in beta power correlate with perceptual and motor demands.
source: Modulations in beta power correlate with perceptual and motor demands (Bauer et al., 2006; Bressler and Richter, 2015; Engel and Fries, 2010; Haegens et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2012; Neuper and Pfurtscheller, 2001; Sacchet et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2008; van Ede et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Abnormalities in beta are a biomarker for neuropathology including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
source: abnormalities in beta are a biomarker for neuropathology (e.g. in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder [Karageorgiou and Vossel, 2017; Khan et al., 2015; Little and Brown, 2014])
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on clinical applications.

claim: High power beta frequency activity (15–29 Hz) emerges as brief events typically lasting <150 ms.
source: In such studies, high power beta frequency activity (15–29 Hz) emerges as brief events typically lasting <150 ms.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing event duration distributions and by citations to prior studies.

claim: Transient beta has been reported in many brain areas including somatosensory, motor, occipital, and frontal neocortex, and basal ganglia structures.
source: Transient beta has been reported in many brain areas including somatosensory (Jones et al., 2009; Sherman et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2010), motor (Feingold et al., 2015; Rule et al., 2017), occipital (Freyer et al., 2009), and frontal neocortex (Lundqvist et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2016), and basal ganglia structures (Bartolo and Merchant, 2015; Feingold et al., 2015; Tinkhauser et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Lower prestimulus beta power (averaged in the 1 s prestimulus time window) in the human primary somatosensory neocortex (SI) predicts an increase in the probability of detection of tactile stimuli at perceptual threshold.
source: We have previously shown, using magnetoencephalography (MEG), that lower prestimulus beta power (averaged in the 1 s prestimulus time window) in the human primary somatosensory neocortex (SI) predicts an increase in the probability of detection of tactile stimuli at perceptual threshold (Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a replication of a prior finding, supported by data in Figure 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Shifts in spatial attention modulate post-cue/prestimulus beta power, such that average power decreases in the attended SI location.
source: Correspondingly, shifts in spatial attention modulate post-cue/prestimulus beta power, such that average power decreases in the attended SI location (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C and citations to previous work.

claim: A lower rate of prestimulus beta events predicts enhanced detection of stimuli at perceptual threshold.
source: A lower rate of prestimulus beta events predicts enhanced detection of stimuli at perceptual threshold
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of beta events in the attended region of the brain decreases.
source: and the rate of beta events in the attended region of the brain decreases.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7C showing attention task results.

claim: Non-detected trials were more likely to have a high-power beta event within approximately 200 ms of the stimulus.
source: Moreover, non-detected trials were more likely to have a high-power beta event within approximately 200 ms of the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing timing relationships.

claim: Beta events are generated by a transient, 'bursty' mechanism rather than being a byproduct of a sustained oscillation whose power gets dynamically modulated.
source: Importantly, these beta events were not a byproduct a sustained oscillation whose power gets dynamically modulated; rather, we find evidence that beta events may be generated by a transient, 'bursty' mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 10, 11, and 12 analyzing rhythmicity and generation mechanisms.

claim: The rate of detection (hit rate) decreases as averaged prestimulus beta power increases in human MEG data.
source: Figure 1Aii illustrates this result, showing that the rate of detection (hit rate, measured as percent change from mean [PCM]) decreases as averaged prestimulus beta power increases.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1Aii with human detection data.

claim: Human detection data were obtained from an MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI in the post-central gyrus in all subjects (N = 10 subjects).
source: Human detection data were obtained from an MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI in the post-central gyrus in all subjects (N = 10 subjects)
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data source.

claim: Beta power recorded as LFP from SI of mice performing a vibrissae task shows a negative relationship to detection.
source: Beta power recorded as LFP from SI of mice performing a similar vibrissae task (Figure 1Bi–ii) also shows a negative relationship to detection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with mouse LFP data.

claim: Mouse LFP data were obtained from the SI 'barrel' neocortex contralateral to the stimulated vibrissae (N = 10 sessions from two mice).
source: These data were obtained from the SI 'barrel' neocortex contralateral to the stimulated vibrissae (N = 10 sessions from two mice)
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data source for mouse experiments.

claim: When human subjects are cued to attend to perceptual-threshold level stimulation in the hand or foot, a negative relationship exists between prestimulus beta power and the allocation of attention.
source: Consistent with this prediction, when human subjects are cued to attend to perceptual-threshold level stimulation in the hand or foot (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015), a similar negative relationship exists between prestimulus beta power and the allocation of attention (attend-in rate, measured as PCM of attend hand trial) (Figure 1Ci–ii
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with human attention task data.

claim: Human attention data were obtained from a MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI (N = 10 subjects).
source: Human attention data were also obtained from a MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI (N = 10 subjects
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data source for attention experiments.

claim: The pooled average prestimulus beta power was significantly higher on non-detected/attend out trials (p<0.05) in all three datasets.
source: All three datasets showed significance, such that the pooled average was significantly higher on non-detected/attend out trials (p<0.05, right-tailed paired t-test).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1iii.

claim: The effect size of the difference in prestimulus beta power across behavioral conditions was larger for detection than attention.
source: Quantification of the corresponding effect size showed the difference across behavioral conditions was larger for detection than attention (see Cohen's d values in Figure 1 panels iii).
evidence: This is based on Cohen's d values calculated from the data and shown in Figure 1iii.

claim: In all three datasets, the median of DP and AP distributions were significantly <0.5, such that higher power indicated the subject was less likely to detect or attend to the stimulus.
source: In all three datasets, the median of DP and AP distributions were significantly <0.5, such that higher power indicated the subject was less likely to detect or attend to the stimulus (Figure 1iv asterisks p<0.05, p-values from one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on ideal observer analysis shown in Figure 1iv.

claim: In 50% of human subjects and mouse sessions, high beta was significantly predictive of non-detection.
source: While this effect was significant in all three datasets, the effect was stronger in the detection datasets, where in 50% of human subjects and mouse sessions high beta was significantly predictive of non-detection
evidence: This is based on bootstrapped confidence interval analysis of DP values shown in Figure 1iv.

claim: Only 10% of the subjects in the attention dataset showed significant predictability of high beta for attend-out trials.
source: as compared to the attention dataset where only 10% of the subjects showed significance
evidence: This is based on bootstrapped confidence interval analysis of AP values shown in Figure 1iv.

claim: Averaged beta power was not significantly higher in correct rejections compared to false alarms across mouse sessions.
source: Averaged beta power was not significantly higher in correct rejections compared to false alarms across sessions, arguing strongly against the possibility that the difference was due to modulation of the criterion or motor readiness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; right-tailed paired t-test).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Beta emerges as a transient surge in power (i.e. events) on individual trials.
source: Beta emerges as a transient surge in power (i.e. events) on individual trials in our data (Figure 2ii).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 showing individual trial spectrograms.

claim: The accumulation of beta events across trials creates a continuous band of activity in the average, often misinterpreted as a sustained rhythm.
source: Because power spectral values are non-negative, the accumulation of events across trials creates a continuous band of activity in the average, often misinterpreted as a sustained rhythm (Figure 2i) (Jones, 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing averaged spectrograms (Figure 2i) with individual trial data (Figure 2ii), and supported by citation.

claim: The correlation between percent area above cutoff in the prestimulus beta band spectrogram and trial mean prestimulus beta power was highest near the 6X median power cutoff across species and behavioral tasks.
source: The correlation with mean power was highest near the 6X median power cutoff across species and behavioral tasks (dotted line in Figure 4i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4i displaying correlation curves for different power cutoffs.

claim: The 6X median cutoff captures approximately 20% of all local maxima in the beta band.
source: The inverse cumulative density function (1-CDF) of all local maxima in the beta band as a function of the power cutoff shows that 6X median cutoff captures ~20% of all local maxima (Figure 4ii).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4ii displaying the 1-CDF curves.

claim: In almost all trials, <4 beta events occurred in the 1 s prestimulus period.
source: In almost all trials,<4 beta events occurred in the 1 s prestimulus period
evidence: This is shown in the event number probability histograms in Figure 5.

claim: The mean event duration across events was 167 ± 1.6 ms for human detection, 145 ± 1.3 ms for mouse detection, and 153 ± 1.4 ms for human attention.
source: the event duration was confined to a restricted range around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 167 ± 1.6 ms; mouse detection 145 ± 1.3 ms; human attention 153 ± 1.4 ms)
evidence: These values are calculated from the event duration distributions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean event frequency span across events was 8.6 ± 0.07 Hz for human detection, 10.6 ± 0.11 Hz for mouse detection, and 8.9 ± 0.07 Hz for human attention.
source: and, the event frequency span was confined around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 8.6 ± 0.07 Hz; mouse detection 10.6 ± 0.11 Hz; human attention 8.9 ± 0.07 Hz).
evidence: These values are calculated from the event frequency span distributions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The correlation coefficient distributions between trial mean prestimulus power and beta event features showed significant differences in all three datasets (Friedman test).
source: The correlation coefficient distributions showed significant differences in all three datasets (Friedman test: human detection p=3.92×10-6, df=3, χ2=27.8; mouse detection p=5.89×10-6, df=3, χ2=27; human attention p=2.33×10-6, df=3, χ2=28.9).
evidence: These statistical test results are reported based on analysis of data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In each dataset, the number of beta events in the prestimulus period showed a significantly higher correlation with trial mean prestimulus beta power than the trial mean event power, duration or frequency span.
source: In each dataset, the number of beta events in the prestimulus period (i.e. rate) showed a significantly higher correlation with trial mean prestimulus beta power than the trial mean event power, duration or frequency span (Figure 6 asterisks denote p<0.05, Holm-Bonferroni corrected post-hoc Wilcoxon signed rank test
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 6 with post-hoc testing.

claim: In the human data, only the number of events per trial was significantly higher in non-detected (miss)/attend out conditions.
source: In the human data, only the number of events per trial was significantly higher in non-detected (miss)/attend out conditions (Figure 7iii, asterisks p<0.05, right-tailed paired t-test)
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 7iii.

claim: In the human data, only the number of events had DP/AP distributions that were significantly less than 0.5 across subjects.
source: and only the number of events had DP/AP distributions that were significantly less than 0.5 across subjects (Figure 7iv, asterisks p<0.05, one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 7iv.

claim: In the mouse LFP dataset, trial mean event power and frequency span were also predictive of non-detection.
source: The number of beta events was also predictive of behavior in the mouse LFP. In this dataset, trial mean event power and frequency span were also predictive of non-detection
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B iii-iv with mouse data.

claim: In all three datasets, the effect size of the difference across behavioral conditions was higher for event number than any other event feature.
source: However, in all three datasets, the effect size of the difference across behavioral conditions was higher for event number than any other event feature (see Cohen's d values in Figure 7iii).
evidence: This is shown by Cohen's d values in Figure 7iii.

claim: The percent of subjects/sessions that had DP/AP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for event number in all three datasets.
source: Further, the percent of subjects/sessions that had DP/AP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for event number in all three datasets (as determined by 95% confidence interval, constructed from bootstrapping 1000 times; see parentheses Figure 7iv).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7iv with bootstrapped confidence intervals.

claim: As the beta event power cutoff was lowered, the trial mean event power became more strongly correlated with mean prestimulus power, while event number became less correlated (the two curves cross at ~3X median cutoff).
source: We found that as the beta event power cutoff was lowered, the trial mean event power became more strongly correlated with mean prestimulus power, while event number became less correlated (the two curves cross at ~3X median cutoff, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 displaying sliding cutoff analysis.

claim: Event power was a stronger predictor of behavior than event number for low power cutoffs (~<3X median).
source: Similarly, event power was a stronger predictor of behavior than event number for low power cutoffs (~<3X median, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 with sliding cutoff analysis.

claim: Trials with zero events were more likely to be detected, and trials with two or more events were more likely not to be detected.
source: These distributions and the corresponding effect size values in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D suggest that trials with zero events were more likely to be detected, and trials with two or more events were more likely not to be detected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 with event number distributions and effect sizes.

claim: The optimal event number criterion was two events for most subjects/sessions (60% of subjects in human and mouse detection, and 50% of subjects in human attention).
source: Consistent with the distributions and effect sizes, in each dataset, the optimal event number criterion was two events for most subjects/sessions (Figure 7–figure supplement 2ii; 60% of subjects in human and mouse detection, and 50% of subjects in human attention).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2ii with optimal criterion analysis.

claim: In trials with one event, the event timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials across human detection subjects.
source: We found that in trials with one event, the event timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials across human detection subjects
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2iii.

claim: In trials with one event, the event timing trended towards significance (p<0.1) for being closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the mouse detection sessions.
source: and trended towards significance (p<0.1) in the mouse detection sessions (right-tailed paired t-test, Figure 7–figure supplement 2iii, A and B).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2iii.

claim: Beta events were more likely to happen closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials, with profiles significantly different out to approximately 200 ms prestimulus in the human and mouse data.
source: The probability time histogram of the 'most recent beta event' per trial showed that beta events were more likely to happen closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials (Figure 8i). The probability time histogram profiles were significantly different out to ~200 ms prestimulus in the human and mouse data
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8i with probability time histograms and statistical testing.

claim: Beta events' influence on function may have an effective period that lasts about 200 ms.
source: suggesting that beta events' influence on function may have an effective period that lasts about ~200 ms (pointwise left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis of timing differences shown in Figure 8i.

claim: In the human data, the 'most recent beta event' timing (relative to the stimulus onset) was the only significant feature predicting detection.
source: In the human data, the 'most recent beta event' timing (relative to the stimulus onset) was the only significant feature, such that the closer the 'most recent beta event' was to the stimulus the less likely the subject was to detect (Figure 8Aii-iv; right-tailed paired t-test comparing the pooled average between behavioral conditions, and one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test of the DP distribution).
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 8A ii-iv.

claim: In the mouse data, the timing of the 'most recent beta event' predicted detection.
source: In the mouse data, the timing of the 'most recent beta event' predicted detection as well (Figure 8Bii-iv).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B ii-iv with mouse data.

claim: The effect size was consistently highest for 'most recent beta event' timing in humans and mice.
source: However, the effect size was consistently highest for 'most recent beta event' timing in humans and mice (Figure 8iii)
evidence: This is shown by Cohen's d values in Figure 8iii.

claim: The percent of subjects/sessions with DP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for 'most recent beta event' timing.
source: and the percent of subjects/sessions with DP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for 'most recent beta event' timing (as determined by 95% confidence interval, constructed from bootstrapping 1000 times; see parentheses Figure 8iv).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8iv with bootstrapped confidence intervals.

claim: After event number matching, the pooled average of 'most recent beta event' timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the human detection dataset (p=0.01).
source: The pooled average of 'most recent beta event' timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the human detection dataset (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.01)
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on event number matched analysis shown in Figure 9i.

claim: After event number matching, the 'most recent beta event' timing trended toward significance (p=0.076) for being closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the mouse detection dataset.
source: and trended toward significance in the mouse detection dataset (p=0.076).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on event number matched analysis shown in Figure 9i.

claim: After 'most recent event' timing matching, the pooled average of event number was significantly higher in the non-detected trials in the mouse dataset (p=0.034).
source: In the mouse dataset, the pooled average of event number was significantly higher in the non-detected trials (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.034)
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on timing matched analysis shown in Figure 9ii.

claim: After 'most recent event' timing matching, event number trended towards significance (p=0.075) for being higher in non-detected trials in the human detection dataset.
source: and trended towards significance in the human detection dataset (p=0.075).
evidence: This statistical result is reported based on timing matched analysis shown in Figure 9ii.

claim: The inter-event interval (IEI) distributions did not differ between detected versus non-detected or attend-in versus attend-out conditions.
source: The IEI distributions did not differ between detected versus non-detected or attend-in versus attend-out conditions (Figure 10i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10i with IEI distributions.

claim: There was no clear evidence in the IEI distribution that beta events occur rhythmically in 1 s prestimulus windows.
source: Moreover, there was no clear evidence in the IEI distribution that beta events occur rhythmically in 1 s prestimulus windows.
evidence: This is based on analysis of IEI distributions shown in Figure 10i.

claim: CV2 was around 1 in all three datasets.
source: In all three datasets, CV2 was around 1 (Figure 10ii).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10ii with CV2 values plotted.

claim: The CV2 distributions were not significantly different from one across human subjects in detection (p=0.106) and attention (p=0.375) tasks.
source: The CV2 distributions were not significantly different from one across human subjects (two-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test: human detection p=0.106; human attention p=0.375)
evidence: These statistical test results are reported based on analysis of CV2 values shown in Figure 10ii.

claim: CV2 trended towards being higher than one across mouse detection sessions (p=0.065).
source: and trended towards being higher than one across mouse detection sessions (p=0.065).
evidence: This statistical test result is reported based on analysis of CV2 values shown in Figure 10ii.

claim: The Fano Factor values were above one in all subjects/sessions across all three datasets (p=9.77×10-4 for all three datasets).
source: The Fano Factor values were above one in all subjects/sessions across all three datasets (Figure 10ii, one-sample right-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test: p=9.77×10-4 for all three datasets).
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 10ii with Fano Factor values.

claim: In each dataset, almost all data points had Fano Factors larger than CV2, indicating that the driver underlying beta event generation was not a renewal process.
source: However, in each dataset, almost all data points had Fano Factors larger than CV2, indicating that the driver underlying beta event generation was not a renewal process.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10ii and interpreted based on renewal process theory.

claim: Most supra-cutoff regions had a single local maximum (~80%).
source: Most supra-cutoff regions had a single local maximum (~80%)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11i with probability histograms of maxima per event.

claim: The probability of a given number of maxima per event was not significantly different across behavioral conditions.
source: and the probability of a given number of maxima per event was not significantly different across behavioral conditions (Figure 11i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11i comparing detected and non-detected conditions.

claim: Neither the detected nor the non-detected (and, attend-in nor attend-out) IEI distributions of 'non-overlapping events' were distinct from the jittered distributions, suggesting that 'non-overlapping beta events' did not occur rhythmically in any behavioral condition.
source: Neither the detected nor the non-detected (and, attend-in nor attend-out) IEI distributions were distinct from the jittered distributions, suggesting that 'non-overlapping beta events' did not occur rhythmically in any behavioral condition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11ii comparing actual and jittered IEI distributions.

claim: With the 'non-overlapping events' definition, event number showed the highest correlation with mean prestimulus power.
source: Results on the relationships between beta event features and power and behavior also held under the 'non-overlapping events' definition, such that event number showed the highest correlation with mean prestimulus power (Figure 11iii)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11iii with correlation analysis.

claim: With the 'non-overlapping events' definition, event number was the most consistent predictor of detection/attention.
source: and was the most consistent predictor of detection/attention (Figure 11iv).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11iv with DP/AP analysis.

claim: The lack of evidence for rhythmicity of beta events, together with the Fano Factors being well over 1, implies that the underlying mechanism generating beta events was less regular than a Poisson process and more akin to a 'bursty' process.
source: The lack of evidence for rhythmicity of beta events (Figure 10i and Figure 11ii), together with the Fano Factors being well over 1 (Figure 10ii), implies that the underlying mechanism generating beta events was less regular than a Poisson process and more akin to a 'bursty' process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical properties shown in Figures 10 and 11.

claim: Under the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis, the rhythmicity of the beta component of the signal would be independent of its amplitude.
source: A Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis predicts the existence of an ongoing continuous rhythm whose amplitude (and hence power) was dynamically modulated. Under this hypothesis, the rhythmicity of the beta component of the signal would be independent of its amplitude.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction used to test competing hypotheses.

claim: Under the Bursty Generator hypothesis, beta rhythmicity is only present when the generator triggers the system, restricted to high beta power regions of the data.
source: In contrast, the Bursty Generator hypothesis assumes that the generator that triggers the beta waveform also causes the transient surge in beta amplitude. Under this hypothesis, beta rhythmicity is only present when this generator triggers the system: If so, rhythmicity would be restricted to high beta power regions of the data.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction used to test competing hypotheses.

claim: Time lags above the amplitude cutoff are integer multiples of the beta period (distributions centered at 0), whereas time lags below cutoff are not (distributions are flat).
source: These probability histograms show that time lags above cutoff are integer multiples of the beta period (i.e. distributions are centered at 0), in direct contrast to time lags below cutoff that are not (i.e. distributions are flat).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12B with modulo probability histograms.

claim: The results strongly support the prediction that high power regions are rhythmic but low power regions are not, providing evidence for the Bursty Generator hypothesis over the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis.
source: Overall, these results strongly support the prediction that high power regions are rhythmic but low power regions are not, providing evidence for the Bursty Generator hypothesis over the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis
evidence: This conclusion is based on the analysis shown in Figure 12.

claim: Averaged prestimulus beta activity in somatosensory neocortex is predictive of perceptual success and shifts in attention, such that higher power reflects decreased detection or attention.
source: Our data showed that averaged prestimulus beta activity in somatosensory neocortex is predictive of perceptual success and shifts in attention, such that higher power reflects decreased detection or attention.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings shown throughout the results section.

claim: The result that averaged prestimulus beta predicts behavior held across various analysis methods, species and recording modalities (human MEG, mouse LFP).
source: This result held across various analysis methods, species and recording modalities (human MEG, mouse LFP)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parallel findings in human and mouse data throughout the results.

claim: The finding that beta predicts behavior is consistent with the general prediction that spontaneous sensorimotor beta acts as, or is the by-product of, an 'inhibitory' process.
source: consistent with the general prediction that spontaneous sensorimotor beta acts as, or is the by-product of, an 'inhibitory' process (Engel and Fries, 2010; Haegens et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010; Linkenkaer-Hansen et al., 2004).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: On individual trials, beta emerged as a brief high-power transient above background noise in the frequency spectrum and was consistent with a 'bursty' process as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a sustained beta oscillation.
source: On individual trials, beta emerged as a brief high-power transient above background noise in the frequency spectrum and was consistent with a 'bursty' process as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a sustained beta oscillation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2, 10, 11, and 12.

claim: The rate of prestimulus beta events was the most consistent predictor of detection and shifts in attention, and most strongly correlated with average prestimulus beta power.
source: Our results showed that the rate of prestimulus beta events was the most consistent predictor of detection and shifts in attention, and most strongly correlated with average prestimulus beta power.
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: An event occurring closer to the stimulus onset was more likely to result in non-detection.
source: Moreover, an event occurring closer to the stimulus onset was more likely to result in non-detection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with timing analysis.

claim: Event number and timing may be independently informative to perception.
source: Analysis of a subset of the data where the number of events, or conversely the timing of the 'most recent beta event', were matched across detected and non-detected trials showed that event number and timing may be independently informative to perception.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 with matched trial analysis.

claim: With shifts in attention, the brain decreases the probability of high-power beta events, and this decrease translates to improved sensory processing in the aligned sensory channel.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that with shifts in attention, the brain decreases the probability of high-power beta events, and this decrease translates to improved sensory processing in the aligned sensory channel.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the attention task findings shown in Figures 1C and 7C.

claim: These are the first results to show that rate of beta events in human neocortical signals is a meaningful predictor of function.
source: To our knowledge, these are the first results to show that rate of beta events in human neocortical signals is a meaningful predictor of function.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings relative to prior literature.

claim: Prior studies in animal models have shown that features of transient beta activity in LFP signals correlate with behavior, including motor and cognitive and working memory processes.
source: Prior studies in animal models have shown that features of transient beta activity in LFP signals correlate with behavior, including motor and cognitive (Bartolo and Merchant, 2015; Feingold et al., 2015) and working memory processes (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homology in beta event characteristics across tasks, recording modalities, and species suggests modulation of beta event rate may be the fundamental feature underlying behaviorally relevant differences in averaged beta power.
source: Homology in beta event characteristics across tasks, recording modalities, and species, suggests modulation of beta event rate may be the fundamental feature underlying behaviorally relevant differences in averaged beta power.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of findings across different experimental conditions.

claim: In spontaneous, prestimulus, anticipatory states it is unlikely that beta's local influence on the filtering of sensory input is through a temporal phase-alignment code.
source: Rather, in all three of our tasks, the precise timing of the sensory stimulus onset is unpredictable for the subject (i.e. randomized design). Under these conditions, our results suggest that the inhibitory correlation between beta and perception may reflect the presence of another process that enhances beta event probability/rate
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and findings.

claim: If a single beta event occurs within 200 ms before the sensory stimulus, the stimulus is less likely to be perceived.
source: Further, if a single beta event occurs within 200 ms before the sensory stimulus, the stimulus is less likely to be perceived
evidence: This is based on the timing analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Beta events could have an inhibitory impact on function for a prolonged period that extends longer than the event duration, a period that could be as long as 200 ms.
source: In this case, beta events could have an inhibitory impact on function for a prolonged period that extends longer than the event duration, a period that could be as long as 200 ms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing analysis in Figure 8.

claim: The circuit-level mechanisms that create beta events recruit an 'inhibitory' process that decreases the relay of sensory information to or from SI.
source: Our findings directly indicate that the circuit-level mechanisms that create beta events recruit an 'inhibitory' process that decreases the relay of sensory information to or from SI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral correlations observed.

claim: The circuit-mechanisms creating high-power beta events consisted of bursts of subthreshold excitatory synaptic drive targeting proximal and distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, such that the distal drive was effectively stronger and lasted ~50 ms.
source: Converging evidence in humans and animals supported a model-derived theory that the circuit-mechanisms creating high-power beta events consisted of bursts of subthreshold excitatory synaptic drive targeting proximal and distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, such that the distal drive was effectively stronger and lasted ~50 ms.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited (Sherman et al., 2016).

claim: Beta's inhibitory impact on function is largely related to the likelihood of observing strong distal drive (event number) and/or the strong distal drive happening closer to the onset of the stimulus ('most recent event' timing).
source: Our present study implies that beta's inhibitory impact on function is largely related to the likelihood of observing this strong distal drive (event number) and/or the strong distal drive happening closer to the onset of the stimulus ('most recent event' timing), in contrast to stronger distal drive (event power), longer lasting drive (event duration) or drive covering a larger frequency span in the spectrogram (event frequency span).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about which event features predict behavior.

claim: The strong distal drive required for beta generation could decrease the efficacy of information processing by supragranular inputs to SI through recruitment of inhibitory neurons in supragranular layers.
source: First, the strong distal drive to SI could decrease the efficacy of information processing by supragranular inputs to SI. One prominent candidate for this mechanism is recruitment of inhibitory neurons in supragranular layers (Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The strong distal drive could alter distal dendritic processes in large layer V neurons, the primary contributor to the MEG signals recorded.
source: Such inputs could also alter distal dendritic processes in large layer V neurons (Larkum, 2013; Murphy et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2016), the primary contributor to the MEG signals recorded.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The generators of the exogenous drive contributing to beta emergence in SI could themselves mediate beta's inhibitory impact on perception at the locale of the exogenous generator, in which case the increase in neocortical beta events represents an epiphenominal reflection of this process.
source: Alternatively, the generators of the exogenous drive contributing to beta emergence in SI (e.g. bursting in thalamic neurons) could themselves mediate beta's inhibitory impact on perception at the locale of the exogenous generator (e.g. through a filtering process in the thalamus), in which case the increase in neocortical beta events represents an epiphenominal reflection of this process.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative mechanism.

claim: The mechanisms of generation of high-power beta events may be distinct from lower-power beta transients, and thus separable in their impact on function.
source: Based on the following, we conjecture that the mechanisms of generation of high-power beta events may be distinct from lower-power beta transients, and thus separable in their impact on function.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on multiple lines of evidence discussed.

claim: High power beta events were stereotyped in their waveforms and in their spectral features (event duration and frequency span).
source: First, high power beta events were stereotyped in their waveforms (Sherman et al., 2016) and in their spectral features, i.e. the event duration and frequency span (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and citation to prior work.

claim: For lower power cutoffs (<~3X median) beta event power is more predictive of averaged prestimulus power and behavior than beta event rate, while for higher cutoffs (>3X median) beta event rate is more predictive.
source: Second, sliding power cutoff analyses showed that despite the lack of clear bimodality in the full distribution of beta event power, there was a clear switch in the relative importance of event features as the beta event power cutoff was varied. For lower power cutoffs (<~3X median) beta event power is more predictive of averaged prestimulus power and behavior than beta event rate, while for higher cutoffs (>3X median) beta event rate is more predictive.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intervals between consecutive high power beta events were consistent with a bursty process, as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a continuous process.
source: Third, we found that the intervals between consecutive high power beta events were consistent with a bursty process, as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a continuous process.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 10, 11, and 12.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the high-power beta events that dominate fluctuations in the averaged prestimulus beta power are distinct in their generation and relationship to function.
source: Taken together, our prior (Sherman et al., 2016) and current results suggest that the mechanisms underlying the high-power beta events that dominate fluctuations in the averaged prestimulus beta power are distinct in their generation and relationship to function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings and prior work.

claim: Transient rhythms emerging for a few cycles have been reported in other bands, including gamma and alpha.
source: Indeed, transient rhythms emerging for a few cycles have been reported in other bands, including gamma (Burns et al., 2011; Greenwood et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016) and alpha (Jones et al., 2009; Sherman et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the human data, power-spectral density analysis shows a single 'bump' in the alpha band (7–14 Hz) and a single bump in the beta band (15–29 Hz); whereas the gamma (30–80 Hz) power is not distinguishable from the 1/fn trend.
source: In our human data, power-spectral density analysis shows a single 'bump' in the alpha band (7–14 Hz) and a single bump in the beta band (15–29 Hz); whereas the gamma (30–80 Hz) power is not distinquishable from the 1/fn trend (Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on power spectral density analysis with citation to prior work.

claim: The bump in the beta band emerges primarily between 18–22 Hz, also known as the beta 2 range, and there is no separate bump for the beta 1 range (typically ~15 Hz).
source: The bump in the beta band emerges primarily between 18–22 Hz, also known as the beta 2 range, and we do not observe a separate bump for the beta 1 range (typically ~15 Hz; [Kopell et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is based on power spectral density analysis.

claim: The isolated increase in the power spectral density in the beta band is indicative of a singular underlying mechanism.
source: We conjecture that this isolated increase in the power spectral density in the beta band is indicative of a singular underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on the spectral analysis.

claim: Alpha and beta have separable correlations with attention and perception.
source: Of note, our data also show high power alpha band activity (Jones et al., 2010; Jones et al., 2009). We have observed that alpha and beta have separable correlations with attention and perception.
evidence: This is based on prior observations cited.

claim: Shifts in averaged alpha power occur sooner after attentional cues than shifts in beta power.
source: Shifts in averaged alpha power occur sooner after attentional cues than shifts in beta power
evidence: This is based on prior observations cited.

claim: Beta showed a stronger linear relationship to detectability than alpha.
source: and beta showed a stronger linear relationship to detectability (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior observations cited.

claim: Causal manipulations using brain stimulation may be more effective if they are designed to match the intermittent character and specific temporal characteristics of the beta events observed.
source: Causal manipulations may be more effective if they are designed to match the intermittent character and specific temporal characteristics of the beta events observed.
evidence: This is a speculation about implications for future brain stimulation studies.

claim: Stimulation protocols that drive two or more events in the 1 s prestimulus period may impair perception, whereas blocking such events may benefit perception.
source: Specifically, stimulation protocols that drive two or more events in the 1 s prestimulus period may impair perception, whereas blocking such events may benefit perception.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings about event number and behavior.

claim: Driving single events could impair throughput in the aligned somatotopic area, but only if it arrives close to the time of the stimulus.
source: Our data predict that driving single events could impair throughput in the aligned somatotopic area, but only if it arrives close to the time of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings about event timing and behavior.
